The Series Method is a language teaching approach that involves presenting a series of connected sentences or passages to learners, gradually increasing in complexity.

6.What is the Focal Skills Method in language teaching?

 The Focal Skills Method is an approach that concentrates on developing specific language skills, such as listening, speaking, reading, or writing, in isolation to achieve proficiency in each skill.

7.What are some benefits of implementing Community Language Learning?

Benefits include increased learner motivation, reduced language anxiety, and the development of communication skills in a meaningful and collaborative context.

8.What is Dogme Language Teaching, and how does it relate to language testing?

Dogme Language Teaching is an approach that prioritizes conversation-driven, materials-light language instruction. In terms of language testing, it focuses on assessing practical communication skills rather than rote memorization.

9.What is language immersion in the context of language learning?

 Language immersion is an educational approach where learners are immersed in an environment where the target language is the primary medium of instruction, fostering natural language acquisition through exposure and practice.

Buddhism and Hazaras: Historical Connection
The Hazaras live in central Afghanistan, mainly in Hazarajat, which includes Bamiyan—a historical Buddhist center before the arrival of Islam. Before converting to Islam, the ancestors of the Hazaras and other people in the region practiced Buddhism, along with influences from Zoroastrianism and other ancient religions.

Buddhist History in Hazarajat (Bamiyan & Surrounding Areas)
Bamiyan as a Buddhist Center (2nd–8th Century CE)

Bamiyan was an important part of the Silk Road, where Buddhist monks built monasteries, stupas, and the famous Bamiyan Buddhas.

Monks from India, China, and Persia traveled through Bamiyan to spread Buddhism.

Hazara Ancestry and Buddhism

Some historians believe Hazaras have mixed ancestry, including Mongol, Persian, and local Central Asian tribes.

Before the Mongol invasion (13th century), many people in Hazarajat may have been Buddhist or influenced by it.

After Islam spread in Afghanistan (7th–9th century), most of these regions converted, and Buddhism declined.

Islamization of Hazarajat

By the 13th–16th century, most Hazaras had converted to Shia Islam, influenced by Persian and Mongol rulers.

Some Buddhist influences remained in Hazara art, culture, and historical sites.

Conclusion
The Hazaras’ ancestors lived in regions with deep Buddhist history, especially Bamiyan. While today they are Muslim (mostly Shia), their homeland still carries Buddhist cultural and historical legacies, like the Bamiyan Buddhas and ancient caves.

In the late 19th century, Emir Abdur Rahman Khan's campaigns resulted in significant massacres and displacement, with reports indicating that over sixty percent of the Hazara population was killed, and many were displaced from their lands. As an Indian, this video left me feeling deeply ashamed. I watched and listened with growing horror to this young lady narrate her harrowing ordeal while she was traveling in India. For whatever little it's worth, I want to apologise to this young woman, Phoebe, for her traumatic experience, and since there is nothing I can really do to mitigate the damage caused to her by the scoundrels she encountered on her tour, I thought I might leave a few suggestions for the future.

For all westerners traveling to India, please make note of the following:

1. If you are a woman, never ever be alone even for a second. It doesn't matter how old you are, or whether you are black or white or anything else. The predators don't discriminate when it comes to abuse, harassment and worse.

Always have some men near you who you feel will be there to stand with you in case you get accosted by predators. I'm sorry, I know that sounds misogynistic and patriarchal, but I'm just saying whatever occurs to me in the interests of safety. Your friends don't even have to be men of your own country, they could be men of any nationality, as long as you feel you can genuinely trust them with your safety and well-being.

2. The moment you feel unsafe, immediately pull out your phone and start taking a video of the people troubling you. That alone might be enough to intimidate any would-be harassers. It may or may not be enough, but it's a start, and it's still better than nothing. This one is actually tricky because I'm fully aware that in a frightening situation this would not occur to most people, as they are too shocked and frightened to respond at all, but if you are prepared for it beforehand, it might be easier to remember in times of crisis.

3. If possible, contact your country's embassy and high commission and seek help the moment something bad happens to you. It might also be a good idea to get in touch with the Indian Police, the government, the Ministry of Tourism etc. Record and document all conversations you have with local authorities, with names and designations if possible. They aren't really going to be very helpful, but again, it's still better than nothing at all, and you never know, someone might decide to step up and take action.

4. Making and sharing Youtube videos like this is an excellent idea. That's one reason I'm commenting here, so that it gets a little more reach. This raises awareness about the situation and ensures that similar or worse things don't happen to other people.

5. Do not, I repeat, DO NOT believe that you are overreacting or being unreasonable, or that you might have possibly done something to provoke this behaviour from other people. You are not responsible for how other people are making you feel. This is especially true of women.

6. If possible, name and shame the people who have harassed you. This one is especially important. It will warn others of who exactly to avoid and what to expect in case anyone runs into these people. Don't be embarassed to take the names of people who have troubled you if you know them, name the business and companies that have caused you distress if you can, and feel free to share any photos and videos you have of these people. It would also be an excellent idea to pass on this evidence to local authorities such as the police. Again, this may or may not be of use, but who knows? It's worth trying.

7. Don't let such experiences shake your confidence or self-esteem. It's normal to be upset and frightened and horrified and even traumatised, but if possible, don't let it harm your opinion of yourself and who you are.

Kathmandu Valley is home to numerous famous Hindu temples, many of which are significant pilgrimage sites. Some of the most notable Hindu temples in the valley include:

Pashupatinath Temple – A UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most important Shiva temples in the world, located on the banks of the Bagmati River.

Dakshinkali Temple – Dedicated to Goddess Kali, located about 22 km from Kathmandu, where animal sacrifices are common during festivals.

Guhyeshwari Temple – A sacred Shakti Peetha dedicated to Goddess Parvati, located near Pashupatinath Temple.

Budhanilkantha Temple – Famous for the large reclining statue of Lord Vishnu resting on a bed of serpents in a pond.

Swayambhunath Stupa (with Harati Mata Temple) – Though primarily a Buddhist site, it includes shrines and temples dedicated to Hindu deities such as Harati Mata (goddess of smallpox and diseases).

Taleju Bhawani Temple – A temple dedicated to the goddess Taleju, located inside the Hanuman Dhoka Durbar Square, historically worshipped by Malla kings.

Changu Narayan Temple – A UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the oldest temples in Nepal, dedicated to Lord Vishnu, located on a hill in Bhaktapur.

Shova Bhagwati Temple – A temple dedicated to Goddess Bhagwati, located near Swayambhu.

Kaal Bhairav Temple – Located in Kathmandu Durbar Square, this temple is dedicated to the fierce form of Lord Shiva.

Ichangu Narayan Temple – Another temple of Lord Vishnu, located in the outskirts of Kathmandu.

Bhadrakali Temple – Dedicated to Goddess Bhadrakali, located near Tundikhel, Kathmandu.

Sankata Temple – A temple dedicated to Goddess Sankata, located at Te Bahal in Kathmandu.

These temples attract thousands of devotees, especially during major Hindu festivals like Maha Shivaratri, Dashain, and Teej.

Foreigner who has lived in Taiwan for nearly 20 years here. You did a great job covering a lot of ground in a very limited amount of time.

Spots I think other foreigners would enjoy that weren't covered here: 

1. Taipei Maokong Gondola to the mountaintop tea huts. It's as magical as it sounds.

2. Taiwan baseball games: one of the most incredible sporting atmospheres I've ever experienced. Personalized songs and dances for each player, which most crowd members have memorized. 

3. Guanziling Hot Springs in Tainan. Highly recommend this hot spring area because not only are the hot springs great, the food is incredible. Taiwan has a "mountain food culture" which is often quite different from what you can find in the lowlands. 

4. Green island. Snorkeling and a hot spring right next to the ocean, where ocean water and hot spring water mix.

5. Taiwan has some of the best tea culture in the world. I personally like 旅行喫茶店 in Taizhong as a place that curates some of the best teas from the island with a very nice atmosphere inside a historic building. The area outside of Sun Moon lake also has fantastic tea culture and some beautiful old tea plantations that are open to the public. 

6. Taidong is a place I could spend several days. Many great hot springs, a beautiful sprawling beach, vibrant Aboriginal culture and a focus on organic and back to the land intentional living. Some of the best organic black wulong tea is produced here. 

Obviously there's tons more but these are just some picks off the top of my head. Heavily tea influenced I realized, but Taiwan is kind of famous for that even in China.

Sydney is actually built around Port Jackson. Captain Cook suggested Botany Bay as a site for the settlement but it was not in the same class as Port Jackson. Sydney has grown down to Botany Bay.

No I did not know that Sydney was originally known as Botany Bay - because it was not.

When Cook first landed on the east coast of Australia, he landed at a large bay he called Botany Bay. The vegetation was totally different to that of Britain, and the 2 botanists aboard suggested it be called Botany Bay.  After Cook moved on, he sailed past the next bay/ harbour which he called Port Jackson.

When the First Fleet arrived, Governor Philip found Botany Bay totally unsuitable for settlement. It was too shallow, exposed to winds and sandy. So Philip took one of the ships and sailed up the coast to find a better location. When he sailed into Port Jackson, he found one of the finest harbours he had ever seen. 

He sailed up the harbour and found a cove with a freshwater stream. He called that cove Sydney Cove. Then he went back to Botany Bay, picked up the rest of the fleet and moved them to Sydney Cove. 

As the settlement grew, it took the name of the cove and became known as Sydney.

However, if you’re going to mention some history of Australia, I would really recommend doing some research of the history including the peoples who have lived in Australia for thousands of years before the colonization, rather than only claiming areas to be founded by Europeans. I understand if you want to add some quick fun-facts about the areas, but the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia often don’t get the acknowledgement they deserve for having existed and taken care of the country for centuries, and they still face serious racism and stereotypes. 
Simply re-phrasing the sentences as the area being colonized by Europeans at the years you mentioned instead of founded by them and adding the indigenous names for the areas (Meanjin for Brisbane, Julaymba for Daintree, and so on) really helps for both accuracy and some acknowledgement.
If anyone reading this is interested in visiting the Brisbane/Gold Coast area, I highly recommend checking out the Black Card (https://www.theblackcard.com.au/) who do Cultural tours at Kurilpa in Meanjin (South Bank in Brisbane) and the Jellurgal Centre (https://www.jellurgal.com.au/) who do (more affordable) Walkabout tours at Jellurgal in the Yugambeh language (specifically Kombumerri peoples') region (Burleigh heads in Gold Coast). Both of which are beautiful places worth a visit! There are also other tours being held around the country where you can learn about the history and culture of the traditional owners and custodians of that specific area (as there are hundreds of different tribes in the country, just as there are several countries in Europe)!

Annecy's Old Town, known as Vieille Ville, is a captivating blend of medieval and Renaissance architecture. The canals, flowing beneath stone bridges, add a unique charm to the town. The streets are lined with pastel-painted houses, filled with restaurants, bakeries, and boutiques. 
*  Château d'Annecy: Perched atop a hill, this imposing castle offers breathtaking views of the Old Town and the surrounding mountains. It houses a museum showcasing local art, archaeology, and ethnology.
* Palais de l'Isle: This historic building, situated on a triangular islet in the Thiou Canal, has served as a residence, courthouse, mint, and prison. It now houses an architectural heritage center.
* Promenade du Thiou: This scenic walk along the Thiou River offers a tranquil escape from the bustling Old Town, leading to more wooded and secluded areas.

The M4 Sherman tank was introduced into service in 1942 and quickly became the backbone of the U.S. Army’s armored forces during World War II. Designed by the American company, the American Locomotive Company (ALCO), the Sherman was a versatile medium tank that balanced firepower, protection, and mobility. With its 75mm M3 gun, the Sherman was capable of engaging infantry, soft targets, and lighter armored vehicles. While it wasn't the most powerful tank on the battlefield, it was highly reliable and could be produced in vast numbers—over 50,000 units were built during the war. This mass production allowed the Allies to have a consistent and steady supply of tanks to replace losses and ensure the success of large-scale operations.

The Sherman’s design focused on ease of production and maintenance, a critical advantage for the U.S. military as they fought a global war. The tank was equipped with a robust engine and featured a simple mechanical design, making it relatively easy for crews to maintain and repair in the field. This design philosophy was key to the Sherman’s longevity, as it allowed the tank to stay operational even when facing heavy enemy fire. The simplicity of its components also made it easier to train tank crews and support personnel, leading to a high degree of operational readiness. This was vital in ensuring that the Sherman was always ready for combat, especially during large offensives such as D-Day and the Battle of the Bulge.

While the M4 Sherman was highly effective in the early stages of the war, its armor was often considered inadequate against the heavier German tanks that emerged later in the conflict, such as the Tiger I and Panther tanks. Initially, the Sherman’s 75mm gun was capable of engaging these German tanks, but as the war progressed, it became clear that the German tanks had superior armor and firepower. To counter this, later versions of the Sherman were upgraded with the 76mm gun, which had better penetration capabilities and was more effective against the newer German tanks. The "Firefly" variant, developed by the British, mounted a powerful 17-pounder gun and proved to be a deadly countermeasure against the German heavy tanks.

Despite its shortcomings in direct tank-to-tank combat, the Sherman was highly effective in supporting infantry and exploiting breakthroughs in enemy lines. Its mobility, particularly on rough terrain, was one of its greatest advantages. Weighing in at around 30 tons, it could travel at speeds of up to 30 miles per hour, providing the ability to quickly advance alongside infantry units and engage a variety of targets. The Sherman also performed admirably in combined arms operations, often working alongside artillery and infantry to defeat enemy forces. Its ability to adapt to different roles, including as a flame tank, recovery vehicle, and even an amphibious assault vehicle, made the M4 Sherman an incredibly versatile and valuable asset throughout the war.

The M4 Sherman’s impact was felt not only on the battlefield but also in the postwar era. After World War II, many nations around the world continued to use the Sherman in various conflicts, and it remained a key part of many national arsenals for decades. The tank also influenced the design of future armored vehicles, with its lessons in mass production, maintenance, and versatility shaping the development of tanks in the Cold War era. While it was far from perfect, the M4 Sherman’s contributions to the Allied victory in World War II cannot be overstated. Its combination of reliability, adaptability, and sheer numbers helped turn the tide of the war, and it remains an iconic symbol of American military engineering and ingenuity.

👍 it’s interesting to see how you think it through. 

I start with my shoes. 3 pair. Usually the travel day is a pair of dressy loafers (easy on & off) plus 2 others - dressy ish but comfy sandals that can double as beach wear and running shoes. 

Once I pick shoes everything else has to work with them. 

3 essential Purses- the personal item is usually my Longchamps LE Pliage and I have a small nylon RFID Baggalini cross body that will disappear into my bigger bag if required. Not counting a neck thing with my passport, cash, credit cards, ID & travel documents that disappears into my top. 

I pack a dressy clutch, and blingy jewelry plus a favourite black silk, lace and beaded wrap to wear with a light black silky top to dress up my black dressy casual pants with. Whether I wear the sandals or the loafers it’s all black and dressy now. 

From then on its daily clothes to fit the occasions and the weather. I’m working with my 3 pairs of shoes & 3 purses which are in my favourite neutral- black. I have a pair of dressy casual black pants and a black silk top already. 

Hot climate: Beach or pool is next- 2 bathing suits and a cover up that will double as a light jacket- my favourite white linen blouse. 2 linen shorts- beige & white plus 3 tank tops in a bright accent, black & white. That white linen blouse will look wonderful with the black linen tank and the dressy black pants so that’s another option. Linen blends work well to resist wrinkles but I like the casual look of linen. I hand wash as needed. 

Cold climate: I have 2 coats that scrunch up into tiny bags - a black down puffer and a navy windbreaker. Those are wonderful to use in winter when travelling somewhere warm as they pack away easily when not needed. 

Travel outfit: usually the black loafers which slip on & off at security but stay on easily if I have to run for a gate. The black dressy casual pants. The dressy black silky tank top, big silk scarf in a colourful print, thin black merino wool cardigan and the Le Pliage plus crossbody. A nice pair of pearl stud earrings which I wear a lot & will be my main jewelry choice. 

For extra warmth I always wear my grey cashmere shawl scarf and black puffer coat but those stuff into my Le Pliage or carry on when I’m not wearing them. I strip down as needed to the tank top (a rayon polyester very breathable blend, that rinses out in a sink, dries quickly) and pants. 

The travel day outfit is elevated enough that I get upgraded to business class at times. I’m pulled together but it’s comfortable. The pants are actually a dressy breathable pair of Ponte knit with an elastic waist and have a little give to them. The top is the silky rib knit rayon blend tank that works for dressed up evenings by adding the silk and lace beaded wrap, the clutch, sandals and blingy earrings. 

Cardigan jackets are the easiest second layers, adding warmth and pulling a look together so I choose 2- the travel day is always the thin black merino and tropical climates the white linen blouse is essential so a nice accent colour or alternate neutral is my second choice. 

Skirts, pants or shorts- pick 3. For each bottom pick 2 tops. 

If it’s cold pick at least 2 wool or cashmere pullovers to go with the pants and several cotton T-shirts for comfort underneath. 

A dress if needed. 

A couple of earrings, another scarf for added colour and print, a folding umbrella in a vivid cheerful colour- hot pink or red so an Uber or taxi can see you easily as the right person. 

I don’t bring my whole skincare routine but I pare down to my absolute essentials. Those makeup eraser cloths eliminate a liquid or balm leaving me pack just a moisturizer that doubles as an eye cream plus an SPF. I buy a body SPF there. 

Makeup is minimal- lately I’ve been using the Merit stuff - especially the stick foundation/concealer and the brush plus bronzer stick, an eyebrow pencil and mascara. A Bobbi Brown eye shadow stick blends with my finger. A lipstick doubles as a cream blush. I like a powder compact with a mirror & I have a retracting brush so touch ups are easy. I pick a neutral daytime lipstick and a classic red, berry or bright shade for evenings. 

One pair sunglasses, 1 watch. A packable sun hat.

You should try Irish sweets/snacks. There are a lot more varieties but the following is what I would recommend:

Cadbury's chocolate (Taste different. Irish cows are mostly grass fed all year - this gives a far richer creamier tasting milk. Hence milk chocolate made in Ireland will taste different even if identical ingredients are used).

Chocolate:
Cadbury’s Mint crisp bar (tastes different to the Christmas bar ‘Winter mint crisp’)
Cadbury’s Golden crisp bar
Cadbury’s Carmello bar (tastes smoother than Carmel bars)
Cadbury’s Tiffin bar
Cadbury’s Dairy Milk bar
Cadbury's snack bar (purple packet)
Skellig's chocolate shards (orange)

Sweets:
Richie's milky mints (milky moos) sweets
Cleave's iced caramels sweets
Silvermints sweets

Soft drinks:
Club orange soft drink
Club Rock shandy soft drink (lemon & orange mixed)
Cidona soft fizzy drink (apple)
Mc Daid’s Football special soft drink (Made in Donegal, sold nationwide in Lidl & Donegal. Drink chilled).

Crisps:
Tayto cheese & onion crisps (red packet)
Tayto salt & vinegar crisps (blue packet)
Tayto ‘Mighty Munch’ sweet & spicy crisps (mild spicy, completely different to the UK’s ‘Monster Munch’ flavours)
Tayto meanies (pickled onion flavour) crisps
Tayto waffles (bacon flavour) crisps
Tayto Snax (mild cheese & onion flavour) crisps
Tayto Rancheros (bacon flavour) crisps
Tayto chipstix (salt & vinegar) crisps
(Tayto in Northern Ireland is a different company)
Keogh's crisps
O'Donnell's crisps
O'Donnell's Ballymaloe Relish & cheddar cheese crisps

Biscuits:
Jacob's Kimberley (soft ginger with marshmallow filling) biscuits
Jacob's Elite Chocolate Kimberley biscuits 
Jacob's Mikado biscuits 
Jacob's coconut creams biscuits

Ice creams (individual) by HB (like Wall’s):
Iceberger (similar to Disney’s Premium sandwich ice cream)
Brunch (Vanilla & strawberry flavoured ice cream coated in biscuit crumble)
Loop the Loop (Lime flavour water ice & lemon flavour sherbet with a chocolate flavour coating)

Barry’s tea
Lyons tea

Ballymaloe Relish

While our travel is more episodic, we only book one way flights even if we are planning a RT. This is especially useful if you need to change the departure or return since the original flights may no longer be available or at significantly higher cost. We use Google Flights to see what options are available, especially if we need to connect. For example, for our current trip in and out of CDG we needed to know how to get to Marrakech. However, we always book directly through an airline and never use OTAs.

My tip for managing trips is a paid service, Award Wallet. Once you link your email address it captures everything from flights and hotels to things Ike excursions and concert tickets. If you are collecting credit card or airline points those accounts can be linked as well allowing you to see all of them in one place. AW provides alerts and reminders and will let you know if there is an itinerary change. The latter might be in an email, but those can be easily missed.

Finally, to find good deals on flights I am a big fan of Thrifty Traveler. We are very opportunistic when it comes to major trips and we booked Qatar QSuites to Bangkok for next January after receiving an alert for a really good points cost.

These regions have so much to offer, from history, nature, and gastronomy to culture and traditions that deserve special attention. Here’s just a glimpse of what you missed:**  

SLAVONIA – THE PLAINS FULL OF LIFE 
Slavonia is not just fields of wheat and corn – it is the heart of continental Croatia, filled with rich history, traditions, and warm-hearted people.  

🏰 **History and Castles:**  
- **Tvrđa in Osijek** – an impressive 18th-century Baroque fortress, one of the best-preserved historical centers in Croatia.  
- **Pejačević Castle in Našice** – a Baroque architectural gem with beautiful gardens.  
- **Eltz Castle in Vukovar** – a symbol of the city, home to important historical exhibits.  
- **Prandau-Normann Castle in Valpovo** – one of the oldest and best-preserved feudal complexes in Croatia.  
- **Požega** – known as the "Golden Valley," featuring a charming baroque square and rich history.  
- **Vinkovci** – the oldest continuously inhabited city in Europe (over 8,000 years of history!).  

🍷 **Wine and Gastronomy:**  
- **Ilok Cellars** – the oldest wine cellars in Croatia, home to 200-year-old barrels and world-famous Traminac wine, once served at the English court.  
- **Kutjevo Cellar** – home to the oldest wine barrel in Europe, dating back to 1232!  
- **Slavonian vineyards** – Ilok, Kutjevo, Feričanci, and Baranja produce some of Croatia’s finest wines.  
- **Famous Restaurants:**  
  - **Đeram (Đakovo)** – offers authentic Slavonian specialties.  
  - **Baranjska kuća (Karanac, Baranja)** – one of the best traditional restaurants in the region.  
  - **Kod Ruže (Osijek)** – known for its rich local cuisine.  
- **Food:** Kulen (spicy cured sausage), fish stew, čobanac (meat stew), smoked ham, homemade bread, and fried dough pastries – a true feast!  

🌳 **Natural Beauty and Eco-Villages:**  
- **Kopački Rit Nature Park** – one of Europe's largest wetland areas, a paradise for nature and bird lovers.  
- **Papuk Nature Park** – a UNESCO Geopark, home to waterfalls, forests, and medieval fortresses.  
- **Slavonian Forests** – famous for their high-quality Slavonian oak, used in the construction of Vienna’s opera and Venice’s docks.  
- **Eco-ethno villages:**  
  - **Karanac** – a picturesque village with traditional Slavonian houses.  
  - **Stara Kapela** – an untouched rural experience with wooden houses and homemade food.  

🏨 **Recommended Accommodation:**  
- **Hotel Osijek (Osijek)** – a modern hotel overlooking the Drava River.  
- **Hotel Dunav (Ilok)** – located by the Danube, perfect for wine lovers.  
- **Pustara Višnjica (Slatina)** – a unique rural estate offering horseback riding and nature retreats.  

🎶 **Culture and Tradition:**  
- Slavonia is the home of **tamburitza music**, a sound that reflects the soul of the region.  
- **Đakovački vezovi** – a traditional folklore and equestrian festival.  
- **Vukovar – the Hero City** – a symbol of resilience and history with fascinating museums.  
- **Wine and Kulen Festival** – a celebration of Slavonian food and wine traditions.  

ZAGORJE – CROATIA’S GREEN FAIRYTALE 
Zagorje is a region of rolling hills, castles, and thermal springs, offering delicious local cuisine and rich history.  

🏰 **Castles and History:**  
- **Trakošćan Castle** – the most beautiful castle in Croatia, situated on a hill overlooking a lake.  
- **Veliki Tabor Castle** – a medieval fortress with legends of Veronika Desinić.  
- **Bežanec, Miljana, Oršić, and Gornja Stubica Castles** – part of Zagorje’s noble past.  
- **Museum of Krapina Neanderthals** – one of the most significant archaeological sites in Europe, where Neanderthal remains were discovered.  

🌿 **Natural Beauty and Thermal Spas:**  
- **Medvednica Nature Park** – home to Zrinski Cave and lush forests.  
- **Thermal Spas:**  
  - **Tuheljske Toplice** – the largest spa complex in Croatia.  
  - **Stubičke Toplice** – known for their therapeutic mineral waters.  
  - **Krapinske Toplice** – a wellness oasis with warm thermal springs.  
- **Green Hills and Vineyards** – perfect for wine roads and scenic views.  

🍷 **Wine and Gastronomy:**  
- **Zagorje Wine Roads** – featuring top wineries such as:  
  - **Bolfan Vinski Vrh** – one of the best wineries in Croatia.  
  - **Bodren Winery** – famous for ice wines.  
- **Famous Restaurants:**  
  - **Vuglec Breg (Krapina)** – a charming rural estate with top-quality local food.  
  - **Grešna Gorica (Desinić)** – a traditional restaurant with a stunning view of Veliki Tabor.  
  - **Zelenjak (Risvica)** – known for its rich selection of traditional dishes.  
- **Food:**  
  - **Zagorski štrukli** – a traditional pastry dish so beloved it has been declared an intangible cultural heritage.  
  - **Turkey with mlinci** – a staple of every holiday table in Zagorje.  
  - **Cabbage pasta, roasted duck, kotlovina** – must-try homemade specialties!  

🎶 **Culture and Tradition:**  
- **Zagorska popevka** – a UNESCO-protected folk singing tradition.  
- **Monument to Matija Gubec** – leader of the Peasant Revolt, a symbol of the fight for justice.  
- **Wine Festivals and Events:**

How ignorant is this? There is no such thing as a Moorish king.  The Berbers and Arabs never ruled “Spain” because Spain as a unified nation did not exist at that time. Instead, there were multiple Christian kingdoms, such as Asturias, León, Castile, and Aragon, that constantly resisted and fought against the Islamic rulers in Al-Andalus, which was the name for the Muslim-controlled regions of the Iberian Peninsula.

The term “Moors” is just a nickname. It was a European term used to describe Muslims mainly Berbers (Amazigh) and Arabs. It is not an ethnic or political identity. The Berbers were the primary force behind the initial conquest of parts of Iberia, and they often fought against the Arab elites who sought to dominate leadership positions.

The Berbers and Arabs did not rule “Spain.” The territories they controlled were organized into caliphates, emirates, and taifas (small independent Muslim states). The Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031) was the most powerful Islamic state in Iberia, but it collapsed into many smaller taifa kingdoms. Meanwhile, Christian kingdoms in the north were constantly pushing southward, reclaiming territory over centuries.

Spain as a country did not exist at that time. The Iberian Peninsula was a patchwork of Christian and Muslim-controlled regions. The idea of a unified “Spain” only emerged after the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, completed the Reconquista in 1492.

The Berber role was significant but often overlooked. While many people assume Arabs dominated Al-Andalus, the Berbers played a central role in ruling, fighting, and administering these lands. The first Muslim forces in Iberia in 711 were primarily Berbers led by Tariq ibn Ziyad. Later Berber dynasties, such as the Almoravids and Almohads, controlled parts of Al-Andalus.

Friesian horses are native to the Netherlands and originated in the province of Friesland: 
History
Friesian horses have been around since the 13th century and were used as war and work horses in medieval times. They were also used in Britannia and are thought to be the ancestors of the British Shire and Fell pony breeds. 
Characteristics
Friesians are known for their black coats, long manes and tails, and feathering on their legs. They are also known for their high-set necks, powerful hindquarters, and expressive faces. 
Uses
Today, Friesians are used for riding and driving. 
Production
Friesian horses are mainly produced in the province of Friesland, where they thrive in the sandy soil and meadow areas. 
Registries
The Friesch Paarden-Stamboek (FPS) is the Netherlands' oldest studbook and the world's authority on Friesian horses. The FPS is highly regulated and has about 15,000 members. 
Sales
Friesians are sold to many countries, including Germany, Austria, France, Mexico, Canada, and America.

Just wanted to comment in case y'all run into tornadoes in your next trip, here's some advice:

1. If you are in a vehicle, get to the nearest shelter asap. If you can't because shelter is too far away or there's not enough time to. Get out of your vehicle and get in a ditch and lie flat in it. The ditch will shelter you from any debris and it's much more difficult for any winds to suction you up out of the ditch. Vehicles are a death sentence to be in in a tornado; same goes for RVs, semis, trailers, and mobile homes.

2. Wherever you are sheltering, stick to the innermost room like a closet and stay away from windows. If there's no innermost room without windows, shelter in a bathtub instead. Stick to the lowest floor possible; basements are the best but ground floor is the second best if a basement isn't an option.

3. When sheltering from an active tornado nearby, try to keep yourself covered with blankets, pillows, a mattress, etc. This is to make sure to save you from any debris or the building collapsing if your shelter gets hit.


And most importantly, keep a weather radio on hand- especially when traveling during tornado season. Keep an eye on the weather and weather updates and plan ahead for any interruptions from bad weather.
